title: Johannes Junius Letter: Most Poignant Document of Witch Persecution
description: Johannes Junius, Burgomaster of Bamberg, was executed for witchcraft on August 6, 1628 after confessing under torture to attending sabbaths and making a pact with the devil. Before his execution, Junius managed to smuggle a letter to his daughter Veronica from prison, describing how he had been tortured until he confessed to things he had not done, how he had named innocent people as his accomplices at the sabbath because the pain was unendurable, and begging his daughter's forgiveness. The letter — discovered in the Bamberg state archives in the nineteenth century — is the most direct surviving first-person account of how torture produced false confessions of witchcraft, written in the immediate aftermath of the experience.
historiographical_note: Carlo Ginzburg's microhistorical methodology finds its most powerful English-language exemplar in the Junius letter — though Ginzburg himself focuses on the benandanti rather than Bamberg. The letter is reproduced in virtually every teaching anthology of witch-trial documents because it achieves what the historian's craft normally cannot: direct testimony from an accused person about the mechanics of confession production. It constitutes decisive evidence for the torture-as-confession-machine argument.
source_method: Original letter in Bamberg state archive; published in Alan Kors and Edward Peters, Witchcraft in Europe (1972 and later editions); secondary scholarship
